verdicts.text: With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code you write is not the code running during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) AWS CDK docs: "Stack synthesis is the process of producing an AWS CloudFormation template and deployment artifacts from a CDK stack... The cloud assembly is what gets deployed." cdk synth outputs the template as YAML (the underlying template is JSON), and CloudFormation deploys it. That confirms CDK code generates an intermediate format, and that format is what gets deployed.
verdicts.framing_note: "Code you write is not the code running during deployment" is the blog's interpretation of synthesis. It holds because CloudFormation runs the synthesized template, not the user's CDK program. Custom resources and Lambda-backed constructs are a small caveat.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) AWS CDK compiles to CloudFormation and only targets AWS. An independent comparison says "CDK is AWS only. If you deploy to GCP or Azure, CDK doesn't help." SST also says it now supports "150+ other providers that allow you to build on any cloud" since dropping CDK. "Nearly impossible" is subjective wording, but it fits these sources.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is an editorial description of why SST switched, and it doesn't cite a source. The AWS-only fact behind it is backed by sources outside Pulumi.

verdicts.text: SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own announcement confirms its earlier versions were built on CDK: "We are working on a new version of SST that's not based on CDK." A third-party write-up (5ly.co) adds that "the first two versions of SST were basically the wrappers and enhancers of AWS CDK." It's well established that CDK supports TypeScript and Python, along with other languages.
verdicts.framing_note: "TypeScript or Python" describes CDK, not SST. CDK also supports Java, C#/.NET and Go, so the list is incomplete but not wrong. SST v2 itself was TypeScript/JavaScript-focused.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK and CloudFormation are AWS-centric, which became a limitation as SST's team expanded beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post supports the multi-cloud part. It says "there is now genuine demand from the SST community wanting to use Cloudflare" and that the CDK & CFN model would need Custom Resources for other providers. It says nothing about on-premises infrastructure. It also frames the driver as demand from the community and users, not the SST team expanding its own focus.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source says the community wants Cloudflare and some users run serverless completely off AWS. The claim turns this into "SST's team expanded beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure," and the on-premises part is not in the source.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The on-premises wording appears only on the live Pulumi blog page under review, not in SST's primary source. SST's post is about serverless/cloud providers like Cloudflare.

verdicts.text: Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.
verdicts.evidence: The How Pulumi IaC Works guide says that on `pulumi up` "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program." As the program runs, the language host sends resource registration requests straight to the deployment engine, which calls providers. The architecture description includes no intermediate template or synthesis step.
verdicts.framing_note: This guide is an editorial docs page, not product source, so it only corroborates the claim. That is why confidence is medium. The claim that there is no intermediary format is inferred from the architecture being described with no synthesis step.

verdicts.text: SST's team migrated SST from CDK to Pulumi, re-implementing higher-level components built on CDK.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog says SST "was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation" and that v3 (Ion) is a new engine using Pulumi. It also says its components "are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation", and that "The components look roughly the same as they do today". This supports the claim that SST rebuilt its CDK-based higher-level components on Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's sources describe the components being rebuilt on Pulumi and Terraform providers with the same API. The phrase "re-implementing higher-level components" is the author's paraphrase, but it follows from what SST wrote.

verdicts.text: A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) I found no independent source for this quote. The only search hit that contains it is the live copy of the blog post under review, which can't count as evidence for itself. A separate Pulumi page confirms that SST's founding engineer (Dax Raad) gave a PulumiUP 2024 talk, "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST", but I couldn't find a transcript with this wording. His Software Huddle podcast transcript has related but different wording ("It's fundamentally a completely different paradigm").
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran queries "SST Pulumi \"natural extension of writing code\"", "SST founding engineer Pulumi \"intuitive and powerful\" quote", "Dax Raad Pulumi \"natural extension of writing code\""; top results didn't independently address the claim (https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/, https://podscripts.co/podcasts/software-huddle/infrastructure-as-code-with-dax-raad)
verdicts.intuition_flag: The quote is credited to a job title, not a named person, and reads like polished marketing copy. It may be a paraphrase of the PulumiUP talk or podcast rather than something he actually said, so the author should confirm the original source (e.g. a talk timestamp).

verdicts.text: Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's own descriptions of Insights focus on visibility into infrastructure resources (search, analytics, discovery, policy compliance). They do not describe it as a tool for debugging deployments. The docs say "Pulumi Insights provides advanced search, analytics, and AI for your infrastructure as code," and Insights & Governance "provides comprehensive cloud visibility and policy enforcement."
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says 'visibility/search/analytics over infrastructure resources,' but the claim says 'visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.' Debugging deployments is closer to Pulumi Cloud update logs/Deployments than to Insights.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Debugging for deployments' reads like generic marketing filler and does not match Insights' actual scope (resource search/discovery/policy).

verdicts.text: Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
verdicts.evidence: Custom providers are real, and Pulumi's docs describe "dynamic resource providers" and "component resources." But "dynamic components" isn't a Pulumi feature name. The dynamic providers doc says: "they are lighter weight than custom providers." The claim seems to blend dynamic providers with components.
verdicts.framing_note: The overall capability (extensibility through providers) is accurate, but the term "dynamic components" is wrong. It should probably say "dynamic providers" or "component resources."
verdicts.intuition_flag: "dynamic components" looks like "dynamic providers" and "component resources" mixed together.

verdicts.text: With CDK/CloudFormation, the SST team often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired functionality.
verdicts.evidence: In its "Moving away from CDK" post, SST describes depending on Lambda-backed Custom Resources to work around CloudFormation's limits. It says "CloudFormation is a black box and CDK has to create these hacks to work around it," and "you'll rely on Custom Resources to share references across" regions.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says CDK itself creates the hacks, and that users (including SST) rely on Lambda-backed Custom Resources. The claim instead says the SST team "often had to resort to" them. The gist holds, but "often" is the blog's wording, not SST's.

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one workflow.
verdicts.evidence: The languages overview says "Pulumi supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL," and its meta description names AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Kubernetes as targets. The claim lists only some of the supported languages, which is accurate. On-premises support comes from providers such as Kubernetes and vSphere, but I didn't confirm those separately in this session.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names 4 of Pulumi's 8 supported languages. Leaving some out doesn't make it inaccurate.

verdicts.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' that covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: pulumi/docs PR #21651 adds the post at the claimed path with the claimed title: "A new blog post at content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md: 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi.'" It says the post covers what "built on the Pulumi engine" means mechanically, and PR #21673 adds the cross-link from this file. I couldn't confirm that #21651 has merged or that the page is live.

verdicts.intuition_flag: This link depends on a companion PR (#21651) that may not have merged yet. If it hasn't, the link will 404 until that post ships.

verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for a new SST deployment engine in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: The future tense is out of date. `gh release list -R sst/sst` shows SST is now on v4 ("v4.17.1 Latest 2026-07-12"), so Ion already shipped as v3 and has since been followed by v4. It is no longer something that "will be released as SST v3" once stable. The main point, that Ion is SST's engine built on Pulumi instead of CDK/CloudFormation, still holds, but the wording should be past tense (e.g., "Ion shipped as SST v3").
verdicts.framing_note: Temporal staleness: the line is future tense ("will be released as SST v3"), but SST's releases are already at v4.x.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The post was updated 2025-03-05 but still describes v3 as unreleased. I couldn't find the exact v3.0.0 release date: v3.0.1 wasn't found, and I didn't try other tags.

verdicts.text: Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: The future-tense claim is out of date. `gh release list -R sst/sst` shows SST is now on v4.x ("v4.17.1 Latest 2026-07-12"), so v3, the version Ion was expected to become, has already shipped and been superseded. I couldn't find a v3.0.0 release tag to confirm directly that v3 was the Ion release.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The post was published 2024-09-25 and updated 2025-03-05, but it still says Ion "will be" released as v3. It needs past-tense wording (Ion became SST v3; current version is v4).

verdicts.text: SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own v3 announcement describes a "new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation," and the SST providers docs say "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers." Independent write-ups add that SST uses the Terraform AWS provider internally through Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: No source was cited, so no framing check applies. The live pulumi.com copy of this post has the same sentence, but that is the page under review and wasn't used as evidence.

verdicts.text: SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs describe the Console as its paid product next to the free open-source framework: "While SST is open-source and free to use, we also have the Console... It's optional and includes a free tier but it's a SaaS service." Its Console docs also say "The Console is completely optional and comes with a free tier" (350 active resources or fewer, then $0.086 per resource).
verdicts.framing_note: SST's docs directly support "optional" and "free tier". "Makes money primarily through" is inferred, not stated: SST presents the Console as its only paid SaaS product next to a free open-source framework, but never says it is the company's main source of revenue.

verdicts.text: The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's official Console docs say: "The Console is completely optional and comes with a free tier." The free tier currently covers workspaces with 350 active resources or fewer.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's own 'What is SST' page says it the same way: "It's optional and includes a free tier but it's a SaaS service."

verdicts.evidence: This is the blog post's own publication date in its front matter. It's metadata the author sets, not something a source can confirm or refute.

verdicts.text: SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls when running `sst deploy`.
verdicts.evidence: The SST post says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi ; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." It also says: "Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3." The fetched text was cut off before the "How Does Ion Work" section, so it doesn't show the "embedded" engine or the `sst deploy` details.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi... as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation" and that Ion becomes SST v3. The claim adds that the engine is "embedded" and runs on `sst deploy`, but that part of the page wasn't in the fetched text.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The post is dated January 2024 and describes v3 as planned, while the claim states it as shipped. The embedded-engine detail is plausible but wasn't in the fetched text.

verdicts.text: Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
verdicts.evidence: The cited nitric.io homepage returned HTTP 200, but it doesn't contain the quoted passage and never mentions Pulumi. The page now promotes Suga instead: "Suga is what came out of it: hosting for agents, apps, and platforms."
verdicts.framing_note: The quote is attributed to Nitric's docs, but the cited URL is the marketing homepage, which doesn't contain it. The claim should link to the specific Nitric docs page (e.g. the providers page) that has the quote.
verdicts.intuition_flag: nitric.io now leads with Suga ("Try Suga"), so Nitric's positioning or the docs quote may be out of date. Check that the quote is still live before publishing.

verdicts.text: Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
verdicts.evidence: Nitric's docs say that "All of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments" through the Automation API. Defang's BYOC CD runs Pulumi: the CLI deploys an app "that uses Pulumi to build your container image and run your service", and its CLI code keeps Pulumi state and backends for the CD task.
verdicts.framing_note: Nitric also ships Terraform-based IaC providers, so only its direct deployment providers go through Pulumi. The claim still holds for the deployments Nitric runs itself.

verdicts.text: SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode, and its release cadence is unchanged.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs still say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine," and GitHub shows SST v4.17.0 released 26 Jun 2026, so the Pulumi dependency and ongoing releases hold up. I found no source that directly compares SST's release cadence before and after OpenCode. A third-party blog (bex.co, Aug 2026) says the opposite: it claims SST has been "in maintenance mode since 2025," with active development moved to OpenCode.
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/docs; https://github.com/sst/sst/releases; https://bex.co/blog/2026/08/22/sst-maintenance-mode-opencode-650k-agent-pivot; WebSearch ran query "SST opencode Pulumi release cadence"
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Release cadence is unchanged" is an unsourced cause-and-effect claim. A third-party blog says SST is in maintenance mode, so the author should add a source or soften the wording.

verdicts.text: SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account, not in Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own state docs say: "The state is generated locally but is backed up to your provider using: 1. A **bucket** to store the state, typically named `sst-state-<hash>`. This is created in the region of your `home`," and "Your state file is uploaded to your `home`." That describes a bucket in the user's own cloud account, not Pulumi Cloud. One caveat: the home can be `aws` or `cloudflare`, so "S3" is only correct when the home is `aws`.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says state goes to a bucket in your `home` provider, and it supports `aws` and `cloudflare` ("Currently `aws` and `cloudflare` are supported"). The claim covers only the AWS case and leaves out the Cloudflare option.

verdicts.text: The SST team has said repeatedly about their own architecture, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own materials say this more than once. The providers docs say "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers," the v3 announcement describes "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform," and the v3 README says "It uses Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation."
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/docs/providers/ ; https://sst.dev/blog/sst-v3/ ; https://github.com/degu-io/ion (mirror of the SST v3 README)
verdicts.framing_note: SST says "built on Pulumi/Terraform"; the claim says "built on the Pulumi engine." SST runs its deployments through Pulumi and uses Terraform providers via Pulumi's bridge, so the claim holds, though the wording leaves out Terraform.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Repeatedly... since the rewrite shipped" is backed by three SST sources (docs, blog, README), not a documented pattern of statements over time.

verdicts.text: SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
verdicts.evidence: The SST homepage shows an `sst.config.ts` that defines SST components (`sst.aws.Service`, `sst.aws.Nextjs`, `sst.aws.Email`) and says: "Deploy everything your app needs with a single config." The truncated body does not name `sst deploy` or the specific component examples (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), though the examples it does show are the same kind of thing.
verdicts.framing_note: The source's "Deploy everything your app needs with a single config" plus the sst.config.ts example supports the core claim. The `sst deploy` command and the listed component types are not in the fetched excerpt.

verdicts.text: The published `platform/package.json` for SST depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).
verdicts.evidence: The fetched package.json lists "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0", "@pulumi/cloudflare": "6.15.0", "@pulumi/command": "1.0.1", "@pulumi/docker-build": "0.0.14", "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0", "@pulumi/random", "@pulumi/tls", and "@pulumiverse/vercel": "4.6.0". That covers every dependency the claim names.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's "and more" covers command, random, and tls, which the file also lists.

verdicts.text: SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers." The config reference says the sst.config.ts run function is where "You can use SST and Pulumi components," and that its outputs display "on sst deploy and sst dev." Together these support both halves: SST components run as Pulumi resources, and sst deploy evaluates sst.config.ts.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs say SST is "built on Pulumi" and has SST/Pulumi components in the run function. The claim describes this as components that "compile into Pulumi resource declarations." That is a loose paraphrase of how Pulumi components work, not a literal compilation step the docs describe.

verdicts.text: In SST's deploy chain, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
verdicts.evidence: Third-party sources confirm SST v3 deploys through Pulumi (e.g., sst.dev: "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform"). Pulumi's docs say the engine "is responsible for computing the set of operations needed to drive the current state of your infrastructure into the desired state." Pulumi's blog adds that the engine "determines the order of actions based on this graph" (a DAG built from resource dependencies).
verdicts.framing_note: General Pulumi engine behavior applies to SST's deploys because SST embeds the engine. Small nuance: by default the engine diffs against the state it has recorded ("existing state"), not live cloud state, unless a refresh runs first.

verdicts.text: Terraform-bridged providers, via Pulumi's Terraform bridge, translate each resource into cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: The cited repo page's tagline confirms what the bridge is for: "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." The prefetched body was cut off, so it doesn't spell out how bridged providers make cloud API calls. That part is still accurate: a bridged provider runs the wrapped Terraform provider's code, and that code calls the cloud APIs.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'Terraform providers bridged into Pulumi'. The claim adds how it works ('translate each resource into cloud API calls'), which the tagline doesn't state but which fits what bridging means.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine owns dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own v3 announcement says its new engine "would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." Third-party write-ups add that SST keeps "Pulumi state (S3 bucket)" and "can deploy to Cloudflare, Vercel, and any other Terraform-supported provider via Pulumi." No source splits the work into dependency resolution, preview/diff and state tracking item by item, but those are standard jobs of the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.framing_note: Sources say SST uses Pulumi for its "providers and deployment engine" and bridged Terraform providers. The claim lists the engine's standard jobs one by one, which follows from that broader statement.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Hundreds of provider APIs" is vague; it's plausible because of Terraform bridging, but SST only lists a subset of providers directly.

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
verdicts.evidence: AWS's own announcements already put CloudFormation above 900 resource types in 2022 ("170+ AWS services spanning over 900 resource types"). A current third-party catalog counts 1,613 types across 280 services. So "hundreds" holds as a lower bound but understates the real number, which is now over a thousand.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Understatement: AWS has about 1,600 CloudFormation resource types (over 1,400 in the Pulumi AWS provider), so "over a thousand" would be more accurate than "hundreds".

verdicts.text: The Pulumi engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi docs list DIY backends that don't need a Pulumi Cloud account: "a 'Do It Yourself' backend that stores state in an object store you manage—AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, ... a PostgreSQL database, or your local filesystem." So the engine can run with no Pulumi account and no Pulumi Cloud backend.
verdicts.framing_note: Docs support 'no Pulumi Cloud account/backend required'; 'any Pulumi-hosted service' is stronger, and SST's setup may make that true in practice.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Any Pulumi-hosted service' may overreach: by default the CLI downloads plugins/providers from get.pulumi.com, which Pulumi hosts, unless they're pre-bundled or come from a mirror.

verdicts.text: Cross-reference: the blog post at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ and the docs page /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exist.
verdicts.evidence: Both targets are in the repo: content/blog/any-terraform-provider/index.md has the title "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi", and content/docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers.md has the title "Use Terraform Providers".

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools in the same way, without requiring Pulumi-hosted services.
verdicts.evidence: The docs say Automation API lets you "drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application instead of invoking the `pulumi` command from a shell" and that it "is part of Pulumi IaC's open source offering". The page doesn't say directly that it works without Pulumi Cloud, but it runs on the open-source CLI and engine, which support self-managed backends.
verdicts.framing_note: The source directly supports the embedding part. The "without Pulumi-hosted services" part is inferred from the "open source offering" wording and self-managed backend support, not stated outright.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: The repo describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That confirms the bridge reuses Terraform providers with Pulumi. It does not say the bridge was built "specifically" for third-party projects like SST.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source says 'A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi', but the claim says it was 'built specifically to let projects like SST reuse' them. The claim adds a design intent that the source doesn't support.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The bridge mainly exists to generate Pulumi's own bridged providers (aws, gcp, and so on). Describing it as built for projects like SST probably misstates its purpose.

verdicts.text: Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
verdicts.evidence: The fetched page (HTTP 200, body cut off) only shows the repo title: "Defang Pulumi providers - Take your app from Docker Compose to a secure and scalable cloud deployment with Pulumi." That supports the Docker Compose part of the claim. The quoted wording "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" does not appear in what was fetched.
verdicts.framing_note: The page title confirms Compose-to-cloud with Pulumi. The exact quote can't be checked because the fetched body was cut off before the README.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is presented as a direct quote. Check that the phrase really appears in the README and isn't the author's own paraphrase.

verdicts.text: Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
verdicts.evidence: SST docs back up the mechanism: its components hide the underlying resources ("You can use these without having to figure out how to work with the underlying Terraform resources"). But no public source measures what share of SST users never write Pulumi code, so the "most users" part can't be checked.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "SST Pulumi users don't need to know Pulumi components"; https://sst.dev/docs
verdicts.framing_note: SST says users *can* skip the underlying resources; the claim says *most users never* write Pulumi code — a usage fact no source provides.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Most SST users" is a user-behavior statistic that probably only SST's own data could back up; consider softening it to "SST users can work entirely in..."

verdicts.text: Within an SST app, resources lacking a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly as raw Pulumi resources and deployed as part of the same app.
verdicts.evidence: The SST config reference says the run function "is where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components", and the All Providers page says "Aside from the built-in components, SST supports any of the 150+ Pulumi and Terraform providers."
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs say Pulumi components can be defined alongside SST components in run(). That covers resources with no SST construct being deployed as part of the same app.

verdicts.text: The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
verdicts.evidence: The cited page (HTTP 200) is OpenCode's homepage. It says nothing about `sst` npm download counts; its only usage figures are about OpenCode itself: "With over 208,000 GitHub stars, 950 contributors, and over 13,000 commits, OpenCode is used and trusted by over 16M developers every month."
verdicts.framing_note: The cited page doesn't cover the claim. The npm package page or npm's downloads API (api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst) is the right place to check this figure.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a precise weekly download count cited to an unrelated page, and the week (September 5-11, 2026) should be checked to make sure it isn't a future date or a year typo.

verdicts.text: opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub star count than SST itself.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page returned HTTP 200, but the pre-fetched body is cut off after the title ("GitHub - anomalyco/opencode: The open source coding agent. · GitHub") and shows no star count. The claim also needs SST's star count, which this page doesn't give.
verdicts.framing_note: No supporting passage was fetched. The claim compares two repos' star counts, but only one repo was cited.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Star counts change over time. To settle this, fetch both github.com/anomalyco/opencode and github.com/sst/sst (or wherever SST now lives) and compare their current star counts.

verdicts.text: SST users are running Pulumi's engine whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.
verdicts.evidence: SST's v3 announcement describes the Pulumi/Terraform stack as its "new deployment engine" and says "there is an AWS provider from Pulumi that's built on Terraform." A third-party write-up adds that Pulumi+Terraform is "only used as an internal engine," so users install only the SST CLI. That means users run Pulumi's engine without writing Pulumi code themselves.
verdicts.framing_note: The sources say SST v3 deploys through an embedded Pulumi engine, which proves the claim that users run Pulumi's engine without writing Pulumi code. The claim's 'SST users' only holds for v3 and later; SST v2 was built on CDK/CloudFormation.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'SST users' without a version is only true for v3 and later; v2 apps still ran on CDK/CloudFormation.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides centrally enforceable guardrails, and Pulumi components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
verdicts.evidence: The link target exists (it's an alias of content/docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud.md). That page supports the Pulumi Cloud and policy parts of the claim: "Policy as code enforcement applied centrally to every update" and an organization is "the primary unit of collaboration" with teams and RBAC. It doesn't cover component sharing, but that part isn't what the link points to.
verdicts.framing_note: The page says Pulumi Cloud is a state backend where organizations group stacks for teams, and policy is enforced "centrally". The claim's "cross-team visibility" is a fair paraphrase of that.

verdicts.text: Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's v3 announcement (dated August 20, 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3" and that the new engine "would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." SST's earlier post says the components "are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: The release date was August 20, 2024. Calling that "mid-2024" is a loose but reasonable description.

verdicts.text: SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: SST's v3 announcement says "there is an AWS provider from Pulumi that's built on Terraform". SST's own docs say built-in components "use Pulumi's AWS provider" and that state "is stored locally and backed up to S3", meaning Pulumi state, not Terraform state. The Terraform bridge embeds provider code in the Pulumi engine and does not call the Terraform CLI, though no single source says that part outright.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's pages say components use Pulumi providers built on Terraform. The claim's "no Terraform CLI/state" part follows from how the bridge works, not from an explicit SST statement.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Defined using Terraform providers" is a bit loose: SST components are Pulumi ComponentResources that wrap Pulumi providers, and most of those providers happen to be bridged from Terraform.

verdicts.text: Yes. SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026 and the `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm. The team's public attention has broadened to include opencode, an open source AI coding agent, but that hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub release page confirms the release date: "thdxr released this · 12 Jul 20:18 · v4.17.1". v4.17.0 came out on 2026-06-26, so this was July 2026, and npm shows 4.17.1 as the latest version. I couldn't confirm the ~796,000 weekly downloads figure. The only figure I found is an undated npmtrends snapshot showing "sst 4.13.1 which has 467,885 weekly downloads". The claims about opencode and release cadence were not checked.
verdicts.source: https://github.com/anomalyco/sst/releases/tag/v4.17.1; https://npmtrends.com/create-serverless-stack-vs-sst; WebSearch ran query "npmtrends sst 4.17 weekly downloads"
verdicts.intuition_flag: The download count changes over time and couldn't be confirmed. Growth from ~468k (at v4.13.1) to 796k is plausible, but a reviewer should check it against api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/sst.

verdicts.text: SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
verdicts.evidence: The shared-infrastructure part is at least partly wrong. SST's own docs describe static `.get()` lookups for resources made in other apps or stages: "If this was created in an SST app or in another stage in the same app, there's a similar static sst.aws.Bucket.get method." They also cover referencing resources "managed by a different team." Nothing found shows SST has policy-as-code, and cross-team visibility wasn't checked (the SST Console may count), so only part of this three-part claim is contradicted.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This bundles three capability claims into one marketing line. The policy-enforcement part is likely true, but sharing infrastructure across apps is documented SST behaviour. Suggest narrowing it to e.g. "no organization-wide policy enforcement or centralized governance".

verdicts.text: The linked post 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
verdicts.evidence: The target post exists with the title "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi". It tells the story from the SST team's point of view: "we'll explore why SST moved to Pulumi, what challenges they overcame". It also embeds an SST video about CDK's limits. A Pulumi employee (sara-huddleston) wrote it, so "from SST's side" describes whose view it tells, not who wrote it.
verdicts.framing_note: Pulumi wrote the post, but it is told from SST's point of view, which fits "from SST's side".

verdicts.text: Cross-reference targets exist: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
verdicts.evidence: All four targets exist in the repo: the SST blog post ("AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi"), the How Pulumi IaC Works guide, the any-terraform-provider post ("Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi"), and the Automation API concepts page (automation-api.md).

verdicts.text: - [Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi](/blog/any-terraform-provider/) — the bridge SST and others build on
verdicts.evidence: The link works, and the page's title matches the anchor text word for word: "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi". The post introduces "support for using any Terraform or OpenTofu provider from within your Pulumi programs" and covers Pulumi's long-standing bridging of Terraform providers, which matches the "bridge" description.
verdicts.framing_note: Link target and title match exactly. The "SST and others build on" wording is the author's own description; the bridge part is backed by the post, but it doesn't mention SST specifically.

verdicts.text: - [Automation API](/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/) — how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does
verdicts.evidence: The link `/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/` goes to content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md, whose front matter reads "title: Automation API" and "meta_desc: The Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic interface for running Pulumi programs without the Pulumi CLI." Several other docs pages link to the same path. I didn't check whether SST embeds Pulumi through Automation API ("the same way SST does"); this confirms only that the link works and matches the label.
verdicts.framing_note: The link text 'Automation API' matches the target page's title.

verdicts.text: [^npm-downloads]: [npm download stats for `sst`](https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/sst), 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
verdicts.evidence: The cited endpoint is a rolling "last-week" window. When fetched it returned a different week: {"downloads":1334575,"start":"2026-09-21","end":"2026-09-27","package":"sst"}. It can't confirm 796,291 downloads for September 5–11, 2026, and it will never show that week again.
verdicts.framing_note: The citation can't hold a fixed-week figure because the URL always returns the latest week. A pinned range such as https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst would let readers check the number.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A rolling "last-week" URL can't back a fixed-week download count, so readers who follow the link will see a different number.
